newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia unable confirm Pol Pot surrender.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia unable confirm Pol Pot surrender.

text.p: Cambodian government officials were unable to confirm on Thursday a day-old Khmer Rouge radio report that hated guerrilla strongman Pol Pot had surrendered to comrades-turned-enemies.
But some leaders said they were optimistic the end of Pol Pot was indeed at hand.
"I would say 90 percent at this stage," Foreign Minister Ung Huot told reporters when asked if he thought the report of Pol Pot's surrender were true.
He said other reports of recent splits and infighting within the rebel group had been confirmed and he was optimistic Pol Pot's surrender would soon be verified.

"I think there's a lot of indications over the last few weeks, and few days. Some of the events have been confirmed," he said. "I hope so (but) better wait a little, a few more days before we can hear properly."

Clandestine Khmer Rouge radio, which is apparently under the control of a rival rebel faction which has broken with the leader of Cambodia's 1975-79 "killing fields" reign of terror, said on Wednesday Pol Pot had surrendered to his former comrades.
The radio gave no further details about his location or his fate, saying only that he had turned himself in to "confess".
The broadcast was repeated on Thursday morning with no fresh information.
"I can't say I believe it or don't believe it," Defence Minister Tea Banh told Reuters. "I'll believe it if I see him."
Diplomats in the capital also said the fate of Pol Pot was still uncertain.
"It's clear that it's unclear," U.S.Ambassador Kenneth Quinn told reporters.
"We just have to wait and see what happens," he said as he and other envoys emerged from a meeting with Ung Huot.
Cambodia's First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said last week the Khmer Rouge had split and most of Pol Pot's supporters had turned against him.
Pol Pot and a small group of loyalists were on the run in northern Cambodia, the prince said.
Ranariddh was not available for comment on Thursday but an aide said the prince welcomed the news if it turned out to be true.
"If it is true it's good for the whole country," said Kong Vibol, deputy chief of Ranariddh's cabinet.
"The result is great for the whole nation but first he must give up all material, military material, weapons, to the royal government," he said.
"He will have to face trial, an international court for genocide," Kong Vibol said.
Cambodia's Second Prime Minster Hun Sen reacted with scepticism to the guerrilla radio report.
The Khmer Rouge government led by Pol Pot was responsible for the deaths of more than a million Cambodians.
Phnom Penh was quiet on Thursday, two days after security men loyal to the two premiers clashed in the city centre. Two of Ranariddh's bodyguards were killed in the 90-minute battle on Tuesday night.
An envoy who met Ung Huot said the diplomats had asked the government to reduce the presence of bodyguards in the city in the interests of maintaining calm.
The two premiers have for months been locked in a bitter feud over power-sharing in their coalition government.
